title: GI Pharmacology
summary: Acid suppression, antiemetics, motility drugs and inflammatory bowel disease therapy.

lessons.title: Acid Suppression

levels.kid: Your stomach makes acid, a strong, sour juice that helps break down food and kills germs. Special cells in the stomach wall pump the acid out, like tiny water pumps. Sometimes too much acid splashes up into the food pipe, and it burns. That is heartburn. Acid can also make sore spots, called ulcers, in the stomach. Some medicines turn off the acid pumps. Others block the doorbell that tells the pumps to start. A few just soak up the acid, like a sponge. Doctors also check for a sneaky germ that likes to live in the stomach and cause ulcers.
levels.hs:
**Parietal cells** in the stomach lining secrete hydrochloric acid using a pump called the **proton pump** (H⁺/K⁺-ATPase). Three signals turn acid on: **histamine**, **gastrin** and **acetylcholine**.

**Drug classes:**
- **Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs):** omeprazole, esomeprazole, pantoprazole, lansoprazole. They switch off the final pump, so they are the strongest. Best taken before a meal.
- **H2 receptor blockers:** famotidine, cimetidine. They block histamine's signal. Weaker than PPIs and the body gets used to them (tolerance) within weeks.
- **Antacids:** calcium carbonate, magnesium and aluminum salts neutralize acid already made. Fast but short-lived.
- **Sucralfate:** forms a protective coating over ulcers.
- **Misoprostol:** a prostaglandin that protects the stomach lining from NSAID damage.

**Uses:** reflux (GERD), ulcers, and preventing ulcers in people taking NSAIDs.

**Helicobacter pylori** is a bacterium that causes most ulcers that are not from NSAIDs. It is cured with a PPI plus antibiotics.

**Long-term PPI risks:** lower absorption of magnesium, vitamin B12, calcium and iron, and more risk of some gut infections such as C. difficile.
levels.college:
**Parietal cell physiology.** Histamine from enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells acts on Gs-coupled H2 receptors (cAMP); acetylcholine on M3 receptors and gastrin on CCK2 receptors raise intracellular Ca²⁺. Gastrin acts mainly by releasing histamine from ECL cells. All pathways converge on insertion and activation of H⁺/K⁺-ATPase in the apical canalicular membrane. Somatostatin from D cells inhibits gastrin and acid.

**PPIs** are weak-base prodrugs that accumulate in the acidic canaliculus, where they undergo acid-catalyzed conversion to a sulfenamide that forms covalent disulfide bonds with cysteines on the pump (Cys813 is key). Because they act only on active pumps, they work best taken before a meal. Inhibition is irreversible, so acid suppression outlasts the short plasma half-life; recovery needs new pump synthesis. Steady-state effect takes several days. Omeprazole and esomeprazole are CYP2C19 substrates and inhibitors; CYP2C19 genotype affects exposure and H. pylori cure rates.

**H2 blockers** competitively block H2 receptors, suppressing nocturnal and basal acid well, but tolerance develops within weeks. Cimetidine inhibits several CYPs and has antiandrogenic effects; famotidine has few interactions.

**Potassium-competitive acid blockers (P-CABs)** such as vonoprazan reversibly block the pump's K⁺ site, do not need acid activation, have rapid onset and stronger acid suppression, and are now used in erosive esophagitis and H. pylori regimens.

**H. pylori therapy.** Bismuth quadruple therapy (PPI, bismuth, tetracycline, metronidazole) is preferred where clarithromycin resistance is common. Test of cure is required, holding PPIs beforehand because they cause false-negative breath and stool tests.

**Adverse effects of long-term PPIs:** hypomagnesemia, B12 deficiency, possibly fractures, C. difficile and other enteric infections, and rebound acid hypersecretion on stopping.
levels.phd:
**Why covalent prodrugs work.** PPIs have pKa values allowing them to cross membranes and then trap in the secretory canaliculus (pH near 1), concentrating a thousandfold. Acid protonation of the benzimidazole triggers rearrangement to a reactive tetracyclic sulfenamide or sulfenic acid that reacts with luminal cysteines. Pantoprazole's lower reactivity at moderate pH makes it more selective for the canaliculus; tenatoprazole and other longer-half-life analogs aimed to suppress nocturnal acid breakthrough, which arises when new pumps are made overnight after the drug is cleared.

**Rebound acid hypersecretion.** Acid suppression removes somatostatin-mediated feedback, raising gastrin, which is trophic to ECL cells, increasing histamine output and parietal cell mass. On withdrawal, this hypertrophied system causes rebound acid symptoms even in healthy volunteers, driving dependence and making deprescribing harder. Chronic hypergastrinemia also causes ECL hyperplasia; in rodents it produced carcinoid tumors, but this has not translated clearly to humans without other predisposition.

**Hypomagnesemia mechanism.** PPIs impair active magnesium absorption through TRPM6/TRPM7 channels in the intestine, probably by changing luminal pH, which affects channel function. Hypomagnesemia can cause secondary hypocalcemia and hypokalemia and QT prolongation.

**Clopidogrel interaction.** Omeprazole inhibits CYP2C19, reducing clopidogrel activation. Pharmacodynamic studies showed reduced platelet inhibition, but randomized outcome data (COGENT) did not show more cardiovascular events. Pantoprazole is still often chosen with clopidogrel as a precaution.

**Association versus causation.** Observational links between PPIs and dementia, kidney disease and mortality are heavily confounded by indication and frailty. A large randomized trial (COMPASS) found no excess harm except possibly enteric infections, an instructive lesson in observational pharmacoepidemiology.
levels.expert:
**Indications that justify long-term PPIs:** Barrett esophagus, severe erosive esophagitis, peptic stricture, ongoing NSAID or antiplatelet therapy in high-bleed-risk patients, and Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. Many patients remain on PPIs with no current indication; deprescribing by tapering or switching to on-demand use is good practice, warning patients about transient rebound symptoms.

**Upper GI bleeding.** For a bleeding ulcer, endoscopy is the main treatment; high-intensity IV PPI after endoscopic therapy reduces rebleeding because clot stability needs a near-neutral gastric pH (pepsin is inactive and platelet aggregation works). Test for H. pylori and eradicate.

**Neurosurgical and ICU relevance.** Stress ulcer prophylaxis is indicated for high-risk critically ill patients: mechanical ventilation beyond a short period, coagulopathy, severe traumatic brain injury or spinal cord injury. Cushing ulcers are classically linked to raised intracranial pressure and brain injury. Unnecessary prophylaxis raises the risks of C. difficile and possibly pneumonia, so it is stopped when risk factors resolve.

**Pitfalls.**
- Stop PPIs before H. pylori breath or stool tests as recommended, or results are falsely negative.
- Check magnesium in patients on long-term PPIs with diuretics or digoxin, or with arrhythmias or seizures.
- Cimetidine has many interactions (warfarin, phenytoin, theophylline); famotidine is cleaner but needs renal adjustment and can cause confusion in older adults.
- Antacids chelate tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, levothyroxine and iron; separate dosing times.
- Misoprostol is contraindicated in pregnancy because it causes uterine contractions.
- Alarm features (weight loss, dysphagia, bleeding, anemia, vomiting) need endoscopy rather than empirical PPI.

keyPoints: PPIs irreversibly block H⁺/K⁺-ATPase; prodrugs activated in acid; take before meals
H2 blockers block histamine; tolerance develops within weeks
P-CABs (vonoprazan) reversibly block the pump's K⁺ site
H. pylori cure: PPI plus antibiotics (bismuth quadruple therapy)
Long-term PPIs: low magnesium, low B12, C. difficile, rebound acid on stopping
Stress ulcer prophylaxis for high-risk ICU patients, including severe brain injury

Healthy outpatient after a minor scalp wound
Stable patient eating normally after a short procedure

advancedTest.explain: Severe brain injury and mechanical ventilation are classic risk factors for stress (Cushing) ulcers.

lessons.title: Antiemetics

levels.kid: Throwing up is your body's alarm system. A spot in your brain is like a guard that checks the blood for poisons. If it finds something bad, or if your ears feel wobbly on a bumpy car ride, it presses the throw-up button. Different things press the button using different chemical messengers, like different keys for different doors. Doctors pick the medicine that blocks the right key. One medicine helps kids feeling sick from cancer treatment. Another helps with car sickness. Some make you sleepy, so doctors choose carefully. Drinking small sips of water helps too, so you don't dry out.
levels.hs:
Vomiting is coordinated by the **vomiting center** in the brainstem. It gets signals from several inputs:

- The **chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ)** in the area postrema, which sits outside the blood-brain barrier and detects toxins and drugs in the blood (dopamine D2, serotonin 5-HT3 and NK1 receptors).
- The **gut**, through the vagus nerve, when it is irritated (serotonin release from gut cells).
- The **inner ear (vestibular system)**, for motion sickness (histamine H1 and acetylcholine receptors).
- Higher brain areas, for anxiety and anticipation.

**Matching drug to cause:**
- **5-HT3 blockers** (ondansetron, granisetron): chemotherapy, after surgery, gastroenteritis.
- **D2 blockers** (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine): many causes; metoclopramide also speeds stomach emptying.
- **NK1 blockers** (aprepitant): chemotherapy, especially delayed vomiting.
- **Antihistamines and anticholinergics** (meclizine, scopolamine patch): motion sickness.
- **Dexamethasone**: added for chemotherapy.

**Side effects:** ondansetron can cause constipation and heart rhythm changes (QT prolongation); D2 blockers can cause muscle spasms and restlessness; antihistamines cause drowsiness.
levels.college:
**Neuroanatomy.** The area postrema (CTZ) is a circumventricular organ with fenestrated capillaries. It projects to the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS), which, with the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus and a distributed central pattern generator in the medulla, coordinates the emetic reflex. Vagal afferents from the gut carry 5-HT3-mediated signals when enterochromaffin cells release serotonin after cytotoxic damage. Vestibular input reaches the NTS via vestibular nuclei and cerebellum, using H1 and M1 receptors.

**5-HT3 antagonists.** 5-HT3 is a ligand-gated cation channel. Ondansetron and granisetron block it peripherally on vagal afferents and centrally in the CTZ/NTS. Palonosetron has higher affinity, a long half-life and allosteric effects that promote receptor internalization, improving control of delayed emesis. Adverse effects: headache, constipation, dose-related QT prolongation.

**D2 antagonists.** Metoclopramide (also 5-HT4 agonist, prokinetic), prochlorperazine, droperidol and haloperidol. They cause extrapyramidal effects (acute dystonia, akathisia), hyperprolactinemia and, with metoclopramide over long periods, tardive dyskinesia. Domperidone barely crosses the blood-brain barrier, so it causes fewer central effects but carries QT risk.

**NK1 antagonists.** Aprepitant (oral), fosaprepitant (IV prodrug) and others block substance P at NK1 receptors centrally, effective against acute and especially delayed chemotherapy-induced emesis. Aprepitant moderately inhibits CYP3A4 and induces CYP2C9, which matters with dexamethasone and warfarin.

**Others.** Dexamethasone (mechanism uncertain), olanzapine (multi-receptor antagonist, now part of highly emetogenic regimens), scopolamine (M antagonist, motion sickness), promethazine and meclizine (H1 with anticholinergic effects). For pregnancy nausea, doxylamine-pyridoxine is first line; ondansetron is an option.
levels.phd:
**Phases of chemotherapy-induced emesis.** Acute emesis (first day) is driven mainly by serotonin released from enterochromaffin cells activating vagal 5-HT3 receptors; delayed emesis (days 2 to 5) is more dependent on central substance P/NK1 signaling, explaining why 5-HT3 antagonists alone fail for delayed symptoms while NK1 antagonists help. Cisplatin is the classic highly emetogenic agent with a biphasic profile.

**Palonosetron pharmacology.** Unlike first-generation setrons, palonosetron binds with positive cooperativity and triggers 5-HT3 receptor internalization, producing prolonged inhibition. It also inhibits crosstalk between 5-HT3 and NK1 pathways, which may explain its relative effect on delayed emesis.

**Receptor structure.** 5-HT3 is a pentameric Cys-loop receptor. Cryo-EM structures show setrons binding the orthosteric site at subunit interfaces, stabilizing a closed pore. 5-HT3A homomers and 5-HT3A/B heteromers differ in conductance and pharmacology; polymorphisms in HTR3B and in CYP2D6 (ultrarapid metabolizers clear ondansetron faster) affect response; CPIC guidance suggests an alternative such as granisetron for CYP2D6 ultrarapid metabolizers.

**Dopamine antagonists and the QT.** Droperidol carries a boxed warning for QT prolongation from hERG blockade, though the clinical risk at antiemetic exposures is debated and droperidol has returned to common emergency use. Domperidone's hERG blockade and peripheral restriction illustrate how a drug can avoid central toxicity yet retain cardiac risk.

**GDF15 and nausea.** The hormone GDF15 acts on GFRAL receptors restricted to the area postrema and NTS. It mediates nausea and appetite loss in cancer cachexia, pregnancy (hyperemesis gravidarum is associated with GDF15 variants and high levels) and with metformin. GFRAL antagonism is an active drug target, a modern example of how area postrema biology still produces new pharmacology.
levels.expert:
**Choose by mechanism and cause.**
- Chemotherapy: guideline regimens are based on emetogenic risk. Highly emetogenic chemotherapy uses a four-drug combination (NK1 antagonist, 5-HT3 antagonist, dexamethasone, olanzapine). Anticipatory nausea responds to good control from the first cycle and to benzodiazepines or behavioral therapy.
- Postoperative nausea and vomiting: prophylaxis based on risk factors (female, non-smoker, history of PONV or motion sickness, postoperative opioids). Combine agents with different mechanisms; do not repeat a failed drug class within a short window.
- Gastroparesis: metoclopramide (shortest effective course).
- Vertigo and motion sickness: antihistamines or scopolamine.
- Raised intracranial pressure: vomiting is a symptom to explain, not just suppress.

**Neurology and neurosurgery pitfalls.**
- Morning headache with vomiting, especially in a child, suggests raised intracranial pressure or a posterior fossa tumor. Treating nausea without imaging can delay diagnosis.
- D2 antagonists cause acute dystonia (oculogyric crisis, torticollis), especially in young patients; treat with an anticholinergic or diphenhydramine. Avoid them in Parkinson disease; ondansetron or domperidone (where available) are preferred.
- Metoclopramide used for prolonged periods risks tardive dyskinesia, sometimes irreversible.
- Scopolamine causes confusion, urinary retention and blurred vision in older adults.

**QT stewardship.** Check baseline ECG and electrolytes when stacking QT-prolonging drugs (ondansetron, droperidol, haloperidol, certain antibiotics). Correct potassium and magnesium.

**Serotonin syndrome.** Rare reports with 5-HT3 antagonists combined with serotonergic drugs; recognize clonus, agitation and hyperthermia.

**Always treat dehydration** and electrolyte losses, and look for the cause: pregnancy, bowel obstruction, diabetic ketoacidosis, medication toxicity, hypercalcemia.

keyPoints: The CTZ (area postrema) lies outside the blood-brain barrier and senses blood-borne toxins
5-HT3 antagonists (ondansetron): chemo, postop, gastroenteritis; QT and constipation
D2 antagonists (metoclopramide): dystonia, akathisia, tardive dyskinesia
NK1 antagonists (aprepitant) target delayed chemotherapy emesis
Motion sickness: H1 antihistamines and scopolamine
Vomiting with morning headache may signal raised intracranial pressure

lessons.title: Laxatives and Antidiarrheals

levels.kid: Your intestines are a long, squishy tube that squeezes food along, like squeezing toothpaste. If things move too slowly, poop gets hard and stuck. That is constipation. Fiber from fruits and veggies and drinking water help a lot. Some medicines pull water into the tube to make poop softer, like a sponge soaking up water. Others give the tube a gentle push. If things move too fast, that is diarrhea. The most important thing then is drinking special salty-sugary water so your body doesn't dry out. Some medicines slow the squeezing down, but doctors don't use them for every tummy bug.
levels.hs:
**Constipation** means infrequent or hard stools. First steps: fiber, fluids, activity. Then laxatives by type:

- **Bulk-forming** (psyllium, methylcellulose): absorb water and add volume. Take with plenty of fluid.
- **Osmotic** (polyethylene glycol, lactulose, magnesium salts): pull water into the bowel.
- **Stimulant** (senna, bisacodyl): make the colon muscles contract.
- **Stool softeners** (docusate): weak on their own.
- **Newer prescription drugs:** linaclotide, lubiprostone and prucalopride for chronic constipation.
- **Peripheral opioid antagonists** (methylnaltrexone, naloxegol): treat constipation caused by opioid pain medicines without blocking pain relief.

**Diarrhea:** the main danger is dehydration. **Oral rehydration solution** uses sodium and glucose together, because the gut absorbs them as a pair, pulling water in with them.

**Antidiarrheals:**
- **Loperamide:** an opioid that acts on the gut but stays out of the brain.
- **Bismuth subsalicylate:** reduces secretion and has antibacterial effects; can turn the tongue and stool black.

Avoid antidiarrheals in bloody diarrhea or high fever, which suggests invasive infection.
levels.college:
**Osmotic agents.** Polyethylene glycol (PEG) is a non-absorbed polymer that retains water isosmotically; PEG-electrolyte solutions are used for bowel preparation. Lactulose is fermented by colonic bacteria to short-chain fatty acids, acidifying the lumen; this traps ammonia as ammonium, which is why lactulose treats hepatic encephalopathy. Magnesium and phosphate salts are osmotic but risk hypermagnesemia in renal failure and phosphate nephropathy, respectively.

**Stimulants.** Bisacodyl and senna (anthraquinone glycosides activated by colonic bacteria) stimulate the myenteric plexus and increase secretion. Chronic senna use causes melanosis coli, a harmless pigmentation.

**Secretagogues.** Linaclotide and plecanatide are guanylate cyclase C agonists, raising cGMP, which activates CFTR chloride secretion and reduces visceral pain. Lubiprostone activates ClC-2 chloride channels. They are contraindicated in young children because of dehydration risk.

**Serotonergic.** Prucalopride is a highly selective 5-HT4 agonist that increases colonic motility without the cardiac effects of older drugs such as cisapride.

**Opioid-induced constipation.** Opioids act on mu receptors in the enteric nervous system. Methylnaltrexone (a quaternary amine), naloxegol (PEGylated naloxone) and naldemedine are peripherally restricted mu antagonists; they are contraindicated in bowel obstruction.

**Antidiarrheals.** Loperamide is a mu agonist kept out of the CNS by P-glycoprotein efflux; it slows transit and increases anal sphincter tone. Diphenoxylate is combined with atropine. Bismuth subsalicylate has antisecretory, anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial effects. Racecadotril inhibits enkephalinase, reducing secretion. Octreotide (somatostatin analog) treats secretory diarrhea from neuroendocrine tumors. Bile acid sequestrants treat bile acid diarrhea after ileal resection. Rifaximin (non-absorbed antibiotic) treats travelers' diarrhea and IBS with diarrhea.
levels.phd:
**The physiology behind oral rehydration.** SGLT1 couples sodium and glucose absorption at a fixed stoichiometry (two Na⁺ per glucose) and carries water with them, even when cAMP-driven chloride secretion through CFTR is maximal, as in cholera toxin action. This discovery, among the most important in 20th-century medicine, explains why oral rehydration works in secretory diarrhea. Reduced-osmolarity formulas lowered stool output and vomiting compared with the original solution, a good example of formulation optimization driven by physiology.

**Toxins and their targets.** Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates Gsα, locking adenylyl cyclase on; heat-stable E. coli toxin activates guanylate cyclase C, the same receptor targeted by linaclotide, whose design was inspired by this toxin and the endogenous peptides guanylin and uroguanylin. Plecanatide mimics uroguanylin's pH sensitivity, acting mainly in the proximal small intestine.

**P-glycoprotein as a safety barrier.** Loperamide is a potent mu agonist whose CNS exclusion depends on P-gp efflux at the blood-brain barrier. Mice lacking P-gp show that the transporter, rather than the molecule's intrinsic chemistry, is what confines loperamide to the gut, a reminder that transporter-based drug interactions can change where a drug acts. This is one reason pharmacists screen loperamide alongside strong P-gp inhibitors.

**Peripheral restriction by design.** Methylnaltrexone adds a permanent positive charge (quaternary nitrogen) to naltrexone, blocking passive diffusion across the blood-brain barrier; naloxegol uses PEG conjugation and is a P-gp substrate. These are classic strategies for separating peripheral from central effects.

**Microbiome.** Lactulose and fiber depend on bacterial fermentation; antibiotics alter their effect. Clostridioides difficile infection is treated with oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin, and recurrent cases with fecal microbiota transplantation or bezlotoxumab, an antibody against toxin B.
levels.expert:
**Constipation workup.** Ask about alarm features: weight loss, rectal bleeding, iron deficiency, recent change in older adults, family history of colon cancer. Review drugs: opioids, anticholinergics, iron, calcium channel blockers (verapamil), ondansetron. Check calcium and thyroid when appropriate.

**Practical choices.**
- PEG is a reliable first choice for children and adults.
- In opioid users, start a stimulant or osmotic laxative at the same time as the opioid; peripheral mu antagonists for refractory cases.
- Avoid magnesium and phosphate laxatives in kidney disease; phosphate enemas can cause severe electrolyte shifts.
- Suspect bowel obstruction or fecal impaction before giving strong stimulants.

**Neuro patients.** Spinal cord injury, Parkinson disease and multiple sclerosis cause neurogenic bowel, managed with scheduled bowel programs (stimulant suppositories, digital stimulation, osmotic agents). Constipation can trigger autonomic dysreflexia in high spinal cord injury: a dangerous surge in blood pressure. Postoperative neurosurgical patients on opioids and immobile need a bowel regimen ordered from day one; straining raises intracranial pressure.

**Diarrhea.**
- Rehydration first; oral rehydration solution is as effective as IV for most mild to moderate dehydration in children.
- Avoid antimotility drugs with bloody diarrhea, fever or suspected Shiga toxin E. coli (risk of hemolytic uremic syndrome) or C. difficile (risk of toxic megacolon).
- Test for C. difficile in hospitalized patients with new diarrhea, especially after antibiotics or PPIs.
- Hepatic encephalopathy: lactulose aimed at a few soft stools daily, plus rifaximin to prevent recurrence.

**Pitfall:** bowel preparation with large volumes in frail or renal patients can cause hyponatremia or volume shifts; choose agents carefully.

keyPoints: Laxative classes: bulk, osmotic (PEG, lactulose), stimulant (senna, bisacodyl), secretagogues
Lactulose traps ammonia as ammonium: used in hepatic encephalopathy
Linaclotide activates guanylate cyclase C; prucalopride is a 5-HT4 agonist
Peripheral mu antagonists (methylnaltrexone) treat opioid-induced constipation
Loperamide is a mu agonist kept out of the brain by P-glycoprotein
Oral rehydration works because SGLT1 co-transports Na⁺ and glucose with water

lessons.title: Prokinetics

levels.kid: After you eat, your stomach squishes food and then pushes it into the intestines, like a baker kneading dough and then passing it along. In some people, the stomach is lazy and slow. Food sits there too long, and they feel full, sick and bloated. Prokinetic medicines are like a coach yelling "keep it moving!" They help the stomach and gut squeeze better so food moves along. Doctors use them carefully because some can make muscles twitch or affect the heart. Eating smaller meals more often, and foods that are easy to digest, also helps a slow stomach.
levels.hs:
**Prokinetics** are drugs that increase coordinated movement (motility) of the gut, mainly to speed **stomach emptying**.

**Gastroparesis** means the stomach empties too slowly without a blockage. It causes nausea, vomiting, early fullness and bloating. The most common causes are diabetes (nerve damage), surgery and some medicines like opioids.

**Main prokinetics:**
- **Metoclopramide:** blocks dopamine D2 receptors (dopamine slows the gut) and stimulates serotonin 5-HT4 receptors. It also stops nausea. Risk: movement problems, including a long-term one called tardive dyskinesia.
- **Erythromycin:** an antibiotic that also activates **motilin** receptors, triggering strong stomach contractions. It works quickly, but the body gets used to it in weeks.
- **Domperidone:** a D2 blocker that mostly stays out of the brain, but it can affect heart rhythm. Not available in every country.
- **Prucalopride:** a 5-HT4 agonist used mainly for chronic constipation.

**Diet** matters too: small, low-fat, low-fiber meals empty faster.

Prokinetics are also used before emergency endoscopy to clear the stomach of blood.
levels.college:
**Motility control.** The enteric nervous system (myenteric plexus) coordinates peristalsis; interstitial cells of Cajal set slow-wave pacing. Acetylcholine from excitatory motor neurons drives contraction; dopamine (D2) inhibits ACh release; serotonin from enterochromaffin cells acts on 5-HT4 receptors on presynaptic cholinergic neurons, enhancing ACh release. In the fasting state, the migrating motor complex (MMC), triggered by motilin from duodenal M cells, sweeps residue through the gut every couple of hours.

**Agents.**
- **Metoclopramide**: D2 antagonist (gut and CTZ), 5-HT4 agonist and weak 5-HT3 antagonist. Increases lower esophageal sphincter tone and gastric emptying. Crosses the blood-brain barrier: acute dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism, hyperprolactinemia, and tardive dyskinesia with prolonged use (boxed warning). Renal clearance; reduce exposure in kidney disease.
- **Domperidone**: peripheral D2 antagonist; the area postrema is outside the blood-brain barrier, so it still has antiemetic action. Risk: QT prolongation and sudden cardiac death, especially with CYP3A4 inhibitors.
- **Macrolides**: erythromycin and azithromycin are motilin receptor agonists. They induce phase III MMC-like contractions. Tachyphylaxis develops through motilin receptor downregulation. Concerns: antibiotic resistance, QT prolongation, CYP3A4 inhibition (erythromycin).
- **5-HT4 agonists**: cisapride and tegaserod were restricted for cardiac and ischemic events (cisapride blocks hERG). Prucalopride is highly selective for 5-HT4 with minimal hERG activity.
- **Bethanechol**: a muscarinic agonist with limited use.

**Gastric emptying scintigraphy** (a four-hour solid meal study) confirms gastroparesis after obstruction is excluded by endoscopy. Opioids and GLP-1 receptor agonists must be considered, since both slow emptying.
levels.phd:
**Selectivity as the lesson of 5-HT4 history.** Cisapride was effective but caused torsades de pointes because it blocks the hERG potassium channel, an off-target effect. Tegaserod's ischemic signal was linked to partial activity at other serotonin receptors and platelet effects. Prucalopride, a benzofuran carboxamide, achieved high 5-HT4 selectivity with hERG affinity far above therapeutic concentrations; large observational safety studies did not show the cardiac signal. This history shaped the modern safety pharmacology pipeline, including early hERG screening and the comprehensive in vitro proarrhythmia assay (CiPA).

**Motilin receptor biology.** The motilin receptor (GPR38) is a Gq-coupled GPCR on smooth muscle and enteric neurons. Erythromycin's macrolide ring binds it independently of antibacterial activity; non-antibiotic motilides (mitemcinal) and small-molecule agonists (camicinal) were developed but faced tachyphylaxis or efficacy issues. Ghrelin, a motilin family member, accelerates emptying; the ghrelin agonist relamorelin improved emptying in trials but symptom benefit was inconsistent.

**Emptying versus symptoms.** A central problem in gastroparesis research is the poor correlation between gastric emptying rate and symptoms. Many patients have overlapping functional dyspepsia, visceral hypersensitivity or impaired fundic accommodation. Antiemetic effects (D2 blockade at the CTZ) may explain much of metoclopramide's symptomatic benefit.

**Tardive dyskinesia mechanism.** Long-term D2 blockade upregulates striatal postsynaptic D2 receptors and causes changes in indirect pathway neurons and oxidative stress; VMAT2 inhibitors (valbenazine, deutetrabenazine) are now approved treatments. Older age and being female are risk factors.

**Pharmacogenomics.** Metoclopramide is metabolized by CYP2D6; poor metabolizers have higher exposure and more extrapyramidal effects.
levels.expert:
**Clinical approach to suspected gastroparesis.**
- Exclude obstruction first (endoscopy).
- Stop drugs that slow emptying when possible: opioids, anticholinergics, GLP-1 receptor agonists.
- Confirm with a proper gastric emptying study (hold motility drugs beforehand, control glucose, since high glucose itself slows emptying).
- Diet: small, frequent, low-fat, low-fiber meals; liquids empty faster than solids.

**Using prokinetics safely.**
- **Metoclopramide**: use the shortest effective course, counsel about movement side effects, stop at the first sign of involuntary movements, and avoid in Parkinson disease, seizure disorders (lowers threshold) and pheochromocytoma (can cause a hypertensive crisis).
- **Erythromycin**: best for short-term or acute use (for example, before endoscopy for upper GI bleeding, where it improves visualization). Check interactions (statins, warfarin, antiepileptics) and QT.
- **Domperidone** (where available): baseline ECG, avoid with QT-prolonging drugs and strong CYP3A4 inhibitors.

**Neuro connections.** Gastroparesis is common in Parkinson disease (autonomic involvement), diabetic autonomic neuropathy and after brainstem injury. In Parkinson disease, delayed emptying causes erratic levodopa absorption and motor fluctuations; domperidone can help where available, while metoclopramide is contraindicated.

**ICU and neurosurgical patients.** Enteral feed intolerance after brain injury is common; short courses of erythromycin or metoclopramide may improve feeding tolerance, with post-pyloric feeding as an alternative.

**Refractory cases:** gastric electrical stimulation or pyloric interventions (botulinum toxin, endoscopic pyloromyotomy) in specialist centers.

keyPoints: Prokinetics speed gastric emptying; used for gastroparesis
Metoclopramide: D2 antagonist + 5-HT4 agonist; tardive dyskinesia warning
Erythromycin activates motilin receptors; rapid tachyphylaxis
Domperidone is peripheral but prolongs QT
Cisapride's hERG block taught the need for selectivity; prucalopride is selective
Opioids and GLP-1 agonists slow emptying and must be considered

lessons.title: Inflammatory Bowel Disease Drugs

levels.kid: Your body has an army, the immune system, that fights germs. In some people, the army gets confused and attacks the inside of their own intestines. That makes the gut sore and swollen, causing tummy pain and diarrhea. This is called inflammatory bowel disease. Doctors use medicines that calm the army down. Some work right on the gut lining like a soothing cream from the inside. Others tell the whole army to relax. Newer ones are like snipers: they block one exact signal the confused soldiers use. Because a calmer army fights germs less, doctors check for infections first.
levels.hs:
**Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)** includes **Crohn disease** (can affect any part of the gut, in patches, through the whole wall) and **ulcerative colitis** (continuous inflammation starting in the rectum, only the inner lining of the colon).

**Drug classes:**
- **Aminosalicylates (5-ASA)** such as mesalamine: act on the gut lining; first-line for mild to moderate ulcerative colitis.
- **Corticosteroids** (prednisone, budesonide): quickly calm flares, but are not used long-term because of side effects (bone loss, high blood sugar, infections).
- **Immunomodulators** (azathioprine, mercaptopurine, methotrexate): keep the disease quiet over time.
- **Biologics:**
  - Anti-TNF antibodies (infliximab, adalimumab)
  - Anti-integrin (vedolizumab), which stops immune cells from entering the gut
  - Anti-IL-12/23 or anti-IL-23 (ustekinumab, risankizumab)
- **Small molecules:** JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib, upadacitinib) and S1P modulators (ozanimod), taken as pills.

**Before starting** strong immune drugs, doctors screen for tuberculosis and hepatitis B and update vaccines, because these drugs raise infection risk.
levels.college:
**Aminosalicylates.** Sulfasalazine is sulfapyridine linked by an azo bond to 5-ASA; colonic bacteria cleave the bond, releasing 5-ASA locally. Sulfapyridine causes most adverse effects (rash, headache, oligospermia, folate malabsorption). Mesalamine formulations use pH-dependent or time-release coatings. 5-ASA likely acts through PPAR-γ activation, NF-κB inhibition and reduced prostaglandin and leukotriene production. Rare interstitial nephritis means renal function is monitored.

**Corticosteroids.** Budesonide has high first-pass hepatic metabolism, limiting systemic exposure: used for ileocecal Crohn disease (controlled ileal release) and ulcerative colitis (colonic release).

**Thiopurines.** Azathioprine is converted to 6-mercaptopurine, then via HGPRT to 6-thioguanine nucleotides (active, incorporated into DNA and inhibiting Rac1 in T cells). TPMT and NUDT15 inactivate or affect pathways; deficient patients develop severe myelosuppression, so genotype or activity is tested before starting. Xanthine oxidase also metabolizes 6-MP: allopurinol dramatically raises thiopurine toxicity. Risks: leukopenia, pancreatitis, hepatotoxicity, lymphoma and non-melanoma skin cancer.

**Biologics.**
- Anti-TNF (infliximab chimeric IV; adalimumab, golimumab, certolizumab): risks include TB reactivation, serious infections, demyelination and antidrug antibodies (lower with concomitant thiopurine).
- Vedolizumab binds α4β7 integrin, blocking binding to MAdCAM-1 on gut endothelium; gut-selective, so systemic immunosuppression is minimal.
- Ustekinumab blocks the shared p40 subunit of IL-12 and IL-23; risankizumab, mirikizumab and guselkumab target p19 (IL-23 specific).

**Small molecules.** JAK inhibitors block cytokine signaling via JAK-STAT; risks include herpes zoster, VTE, lipid rises and major cardiovascular events (boxed warnings from studies in rheumatoid arthritis). S1P receptor modulators (ozanimod, etrasimod) trap lymphocytes in lymph nodes; they can cause bradycardia and macular edema.
levels.phd:
**Why natalizumab gave way to vedolizumab.** Natalizumab blocks α4 integrin, inhibiting both α4β1/VCAM-1 (brain trafficking) and α4β7/MAdCAM-1 (gut trafficking). By blocking immune surveillance of the CNS, it permits JC virus reactivation and progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML). Vedolizumab's α4β7 selectivity spares brain surveillance; PML has not been convincingly linked to it. This is a textbook example of improving safety by narrowing the molecular target, and it connects gut and neuro pharmacology directly.

**The IL-23/Th17 axis.** Genome-wide association studies identified IL23R variants (the protective R381Q variant), NOD2 (Crohn disease), ATG16L1 and IRGM (autophagy), linking microbial sensing and barrier defense to IBD. IL-23 sustains pathogenic Th17 and innate lymphoid cells. Paradoxically, IL-17A blockade worsened Crohn disease in trials, probably because IL-17 maintains epithelial barrier function, while blocking upstream IL-23 works. This shows that pathway position matters: blocking a cytokine with protective local functions can backfire.

**Pharmacokinetics of biologics.** Monoclonal antibodies are cleared by target-mediated drug disposition and by proteolysis, rescued from lysosomes by FcRn recycling. In severe colitis, protein loss into stool and high TNF burden accelerate infliximab clearance, explaining why accelerated induction and therapeutic drug monitoring are used. Antidrug antibodies speed clearance and cause loss of response; proactive drug-level monitoring is an evolving strategy.

**JAK selectivity.** Tofacitinib preferentially inhibits JAK1/JAK3; upadacitinib is JAK1-selective. The ORAL Surveillance trial in rheumatoid arthritis patients aged 50 or older with cardiovascular risk found more cancer and cardiovascular events than with TNF inhibitors, reshaping labels across the class even though selectivity differs.
levels.expert:
**Treatment strategy.** Modern IBD care aims for deep remission (clinical, biochemical with fecal calprotectin and CRP, and endoscopic healing), not just symptom control. Patients with high-risk features (young age at diagnosis, extensive disease, perianal Crohn disease, deep ulcers) are started early on effective advanced therapy rather than climbing slowly through steps.

**Pre-treatment checklist.** Screen for latent TB (interferon-gamma release assay and chest imaging), hepatitis B serology, HIV, varicella immunity; give inactivated vaccines and avoid live vaccines once immunosuppressed; check TPMT/NUDT15 before thiopurines.

**Acute severe ulcerative colitis.** Hospitalize, give IV steroids, exclude C. difficile and CMV, start VTE prophylaxis (IBD flares are prothrombotic). If there is no response by around day three, rescue therapy with infliximab or ciclosporin, or colectomy, is planned with surgeons.

**Neuro pitfalls.**
- Anti-TNF drugs can trigger or unmask demyelinating disease; avoid in patients with multiple sclerosis or optic neuritis.
- New neurological deficits in an immunosuppressed patient need MRI to look for PML, opportunistic infection or lymphoma.
- Ciclosporin can cause seizures and posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome, especially with low magnesium or cholesterol.
- Metronidazole, used for perianal Crohn disease, causes peripheral neuropathy with prolonged courses.
- Long courses of steroids cause bone loss, mood disturbance and adrenal suppression.

**Monitoring.** Blood counts and liver tests on thiopurines and methotrexate; lipids on JAK inhibitors; ECG history and eye review for S1P modulators; skin checks for cancer on thiopurines. Methotrexate is teratogenic, and pregnancy planning is part of therapy selection.

keyPoints: Crohn disease: patchy, transmural, any segment; UC: continuous mucosal colitis from the rectum
5-ASA (mesalamine) for mild-moderate UC; sulfasalazine side effects come from sulfapyridine
Thiopurines: test TPMT/NUDT15; allopurinol greatly raises toxicity
Anti-TNF: screen TB/hepatitis B; avoid in demyelinating disease
Vedolizumab (α4β7) is gut-selective and spares brain surveillance (unlike natalizumab)
JAK inhibitors: zoster, VTE, cardiovascular warnings
